newsitem.title: USA: Lawyers argue jury queries in Broin tobacco suit.
newsitem.headline: Lawyers argue jury queries in Broin tobacco suit.

text.p: Potential jurors in a class-action lawsuit over the consequences of breathing secondhand cigarette smoke may be asked questions ranging from their personal smoking histories to their ownership of land in tobacco-producing states, a Florida judge said on Monday.

Plaintiffs' and defense lawyers spent more than two hours during a pre-trial hearing discussing the queries and format to be included in a questionnaire to the jury pool in the lawsuit known as Broin v. Philip Morris Cos Inc.

The suit, filed by a group of flight attendants who claim they were sickened by secondhand smoke while they worked on U.S.-based aircraft, is scheduled for trial June 2. The class may represent as many as 60,000 current and former flight attendants.

In a ruling sent to lawyers during the weekend, Dade County Judge Robert Kaye denied a tobacco industry motion for a trial postponement. He said the plaintiffs' agreement to shorten its witness and evidence list would allow the trial to go ahead as planned.

Though the jury questionnaire was not finalized, lawyers agreed the potential jurors could be asked about their beliefs on whether smoking causes disease, whether secondhand smoke causes disease, whether smokers have the right to smoke in public places and whether tobacco companies should be responsible for damage caused by cigarette smoking.
Jurors will also likely be asked questions about their personal smoking histories, including whether they had ever quit smoking and at what age.

Industry lawyers objected when the plaintiffs said they wanted to probe jurors' attitudes toward addiction, saying they were not relevant to a case in which the flight attendants claim they were injured by secondhand smoke.
"Issues of addiction are not issues in this case," defense attorney Edward Moss said.
But Judge Kaye said such questions could be included because the questionnaire was meant to sense jurors' opinions about smoking.
"I don't have any problems with any of these kinds of questions," Kaye said.
The jurors also likely will be asked if they have an interest in real estate in tobacco-producing states.
"That's a good question," Kaye said, pointing out that a juror who owned land in a tobacco state could be concerned with the impact of a verdict against the industry on his or her property interests.
"Maybe you have an interest in whether the tobacco industry survives," he said.

Jurors also will be asked, near the beginning of the questionnaire, whether they are literate in English, a key question in Dade County where Spanish is the language spoken in a majority of households.
Lawyers were to finalize the questionnaire this week. It will be presented to members of the jury pool late next week to help winnow the pool before jury selection begins on June 2.
